hints: Focus on the nature of the two particles involved, a fully charged metal ion and a neutral but polar water molecule.
Remember that in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ the oxygen end is $\delta-$ and the metal cation is fully positive, so the oxygen points toward the cation.
Think of the special name given to the attraction between a full ion and the oppositely charged end of a polar solvent molecule during hydration.
walkthrough:
**Identify the two players**

Think side by side with me. A metal cation, like $\text{Na}^+$ or $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, carries a full positive charge. Water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, is neutral but polar, with $\delta-$ on oxygen and $\delta+$ on hydrogen.

**Match to the type of force**

A force between two neutral dipoles is dipole-dipole. A force between a full ion and a partial charge on a dipole has its own name:
$$\text{ion (full charge) + dipole (partial charge) } \rightarrow \text{ ion-dipole interaction}$$

**Picture hydration in solution**

In water, the $\delta-$ oxygen atoms surround and are attracted to the positive cation. That hydration attraction holding the shell of water around the ion is the ion-dipole interaction.

options.A: Dipole-dipole interactions occur between two neutral polar molecules, such as between two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules. Here one particle is a fully charged ion, not a dipole, so this label is too weak and incorrect.
options.B: Hydrogen bonds occur when H attached to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule. A metal cation has no hydrogen and no lone pair to accept one, it is attracted to the oxygen lone pairs by ion to dipole force instead.
options.C: Correct. The full positive charge of the metal cation attracts the $\delta-$ oxygen end of polar water molecules. This ion to partial charge attraction is exactly an ion-dipole interaction and is responsible for hydration of cations.
options.D: Ionic bonds are the strong electrostatic lattice forces between oppositely charged ions in a solid, e.g. $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$. Water is neutral, not an anion, so no ionic bond forms, only a weaker ion-solvent attraction.
